stories.title: China develops missile to target planes thousands of kilometres away
stories.summary: China has developed hypersonic glide vehicles that carry air-to-air missiles, capable of striking high-value targets thousands of kilometres away, threatening US military operations. China’s missile arsenal, the largest in the world with over 3,150 ballistic missiles, now includes missiles with extended air-to-air and anti-ship capabilities. Using ballistic missiles for air targets is complex and risky, as long travel time demands precise targeting and may risk nuclear misinterpretation during conflict. The Chinese military has developed hypersonic glide vehicles that can launch air-to-air weapons, an advancement meant to threaten high-value targets such as command-and-control aircraft thousands of kilometres away. The breakthrough is part of a larger effort by China to use its missile arsenal – the world’s largest at more than 3,150 ballistic weapons – for nearly every military task, according to a person with direct knowledge of the matter. Meanwhile, the US is struggling with supplies of crucial air defence missiles and long-range strike weapons after six months of war with Iran. China also added air-to-air capabilities to some hypersonic cruise missiles and built anti-ship capabilities into several types of missiles, said the person, who asked not to be identified because of the sensitivity of the information. Such weapons would pose a serious threat to US air operations during a conflict with China. Support aircraft such as tankers, airborne warning-and-control planes and even flying command posts such as the E-4B Nightwatch are meant to operate far from combat. A hypersonic glide vehicle deployed from a DF-17 missile could travel about 2,414km – just short of the distance from China to the US territory of Guam, a major military site. The DF-27 missile has a maximum range of about 8,000km, putting Hawaii in range. Hypersonic glide vehicles, or HGVs, are warheads that can manoeuvre in the atmosphere on their way to a target, extending range and complicating interception.

stories.title: Japan enlists 1,800 people to drag a 360-tonne castle keep using ropes and rollers
stories.summary: After repairs to Hirosaki Castle in Aomori prefecture, officials employed a technique known as hikiya to move the structure more than two metres To chants of “so-re, so-re”, about 1,800 people came together in northern Japan over the weekend to pull a 360-tonne castle keep a little more than two metres closer to its original resting place as part of ongoing renovations. The keep – a fortified tower within a castle – had to be moved to repair a wall that was damaged in a major earthquake. Continue reading...
